paragraphs.heading: The slice we can see
paragraphs.text: The visible spectrum is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that human eyes can see, and radiation in it is called visible light. A typical eye responds to wavelengths from about 380 to about 750 nanometers, which is a frequency band near 400–790 terahertz. These edges are not sharp and can vary from person to person. In the best conditions, sight can stretch to 310 nm in the ultraviolet and 1100 nm in the near infrared.

paragraphs.heading: Colors the spectrum lacks
paragraphs.text: Colors made by a single wavelength, or a narrow band of them, are called spectral colors, or pure colors. The spectrum runs smoothly, with no clear border where one color ends and the next begins. Yet it does not hold every color people can tell apart. Pink, and purples such as magenta, are missing, because they can only be made by mixing several wavelengths.

paragraphs.heading: Through the air
paragraphs.text: Visible light passes through Earth's atmosphere largely unweakened, through a region called the optical window. Clean air scatters blue light more than red, which is why the midday sky looks blue, while near the Sun it looks white because the light there is not scattered as much. The visible range of most animals evolved to match this window.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's prism
paragraphs.text: In the 17th century, Isaac Newton found that prisms could split white light apart and put it back together. When a narrow beam of sunlight hit a glass prism at an angle, part of it passed through and came out as bands of different colors. He pictured light as particles of different colors, with red moving faster than violet in glass, so that red is bent less sharply than violet. In 1671 he became the first to put the word spectrum, Latin for appearance, into print with this meaning.

paragraphs.heading: The trouble with indigo
paragraphs.text: Newton first named six colors, then added indigo as a seventh because he believed seven was a perfect number. The eye is fairly insensitive to indigo, and some people with otherwise good sight cannot tell it from blue and violet. For that reason some writers, Isaac Asimov among them, suggest indigo is just a shade of blue or violet. Comparing Newton's observations with a modern image of the spectrum suggests his indigo is what we now call blue, and his blue is our cyan.

paragraphs.heading: Limits set by the eye
paragraphs.text: To be seen, a wavelength must both reach the retina and excite a visual opsin, setting off the process of vision. Blindness to ultraviolet is generally set by what passes through the lens, and blindness to infrared by how sensitive the opsins are. People have two visual systems: photopic vision for daylight, run by cone cells, and scotopic vision for dim light, run by rod cells. Each has a different visible range, but talk of the visible range usually assumes photopic vision.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the colors
paragraphs.text: In the early 19th century the idea of a visible spectrum sharpened as light beyond it was found: infrared by William Herschel and ultraviolet by Johann Wilhelm Ritter. In 1802 Thomas Young became the first person to measure the wavelengths of different colors. Young and Hermann von Helmholtz also explored how the spectrum relates to color vision, rightly proposing that the eye uses three distinct receptors to see color.
